books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the account of personal liberty laws, vigilance committees, and Ableman v. Booth (1859) in Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 7, Topic 5.5. The facts are as stated in the book; the wording is original.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase: After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, many Northern states passed personal liberty laws to protect people claimed as fugitives, offering them lawyers and jury trials. Northern vigilance committees also formed to warn Black residents when slave catchers came to town. The Supreme Court answered in Ableman v. Booth (1859), ruling that federal law stood above state law and state courts could not free people the federal law had claimed.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Northern states passed personal liberty laws most directly to

options.text: shield accused runaways from slave catchers.
help slave catchers return fugitives faster.
options.misconception: The laws did the opposite: they gave the accused lawyers and jury trials, slowing the catchers down, not speeding them up.

options.text: ban all immigration to the North.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the laws concerned fugitives from slavery, not immigrants; immigration law was a separate fight.

options.text: end slavery in the Southern states.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Northern states could not end slavery in the South; the laws shielded people within their own borders.

rationales.A: Lawyers and jury trials for people claimed as fugitives are shields, and the laws were written to hold those shields up against the catchers.
rationales.B: The laws did the opposite: they gave the accused lawyers and jury trials, slowing the catchers down, not speeding them up.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the laws concerned fugitives from slavery, not immigrants; immigration law was a separate fight.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Northern states could not end slavery in the South; the laws shielded people within their own borders.
rationales.general:
1. Name the threat: after 1850, slave catchers could seize people in Northern cities.
2. Read the laws’ tools: lawyers and jury trials for anyone claimed as a fugitive.
3. Name the purpose: protection, offered by Northern states against a federal law they distrusted.
Remember: when a state passes a law to blunt a federal law, ask whom the state is shielding.
